subject: biology
title: Neurobiology (HL) Adventure 2: Synapses and brain regions
welcome_lead: Today you'll cross the synapse and map regions of the brain.
meta_desc: Biology HL — synapse, neurotransmitters, summation, brain regions, cerebrum.
final_note: You learned synapses use neurotransmitters, EPSPs and IPSPs sum to threshold, and brain regions specialise (cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem, hypothalamus).

walkthroughs.body_html:
AP reaches presynaptic terminal → opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.

Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion → neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) released.

Diffuses across cleft (~20 nm) → binds ligand-gated receptors → Na⁺ in (excitatory) or Cl⁻ in (inhibitory).

One EPSP is small (~1 mV). Multiple inputs sum:

- Temporal — same neuron fires repeatedly.
- Spatial — many neurons fire onto the same target.

If total depolarisation reaches threshold (-55 mV), AP fires. IPSPs (GABA) hyperpolarise — make firing harder.

- Cerebrum (largest) — cortex for thought, sensory, motor.
- Cerebellum — coordination, balance.
- Hypothalamus — homeostasis, links to pituitary.
- Pituitary — endocrine 'master gland'.
- Medulla — breathing, heart rate.

fMRI shows local blood flow → mapping function — opened modern neuroscience but raises ethical questions (mind-reading, court evidence).

What is the difference between a silent and a missense mutation?
options: Missense and silent mutations always produce a non-functional protein.
A silent mutation changes a base but the codon still codes for the same amino acid; a missense mutation changes the amino acid encoded.
DNA ligase reads the gene and translates it into protein.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: DNA ligase reads the gene and translates it into protein.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.
No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).

options: It forms phosphodiester bonds that join the gene to the cut plasmid, sealing the recombinant DNA.
DNA ligase cuts the plasmid open so the gene can be inserted.
